title: Lesson 16: The Crowning Gem (Advanced Division)
subtopics: Single Figure on the Flag Division
Negative Flag Digits with Bar Numbers
learningGoals: Use one-line division by two-figure divisors.
Handle advanced division with flag and bar digits.
coreIdeas: Teach one visual pattern at a time, then checkpoint immediately.
Use active recall: student states next step before final answer.
Keep board, voice, and feedback in one continuous loop.

workedExamples.question: How does 132 / 11 become 12 in flag division?
workedExamples.method: With divisor 11, the leading digit 1 is brought down and the running total with the next digit gives the next quotient digit. The answer is exact: 12.

workedExamples.question: How does 253 / 12 give 21 remainder 1?
workedExamples.method: Use 12 as 1 with flag 2. Bring down 2, use the flag to control the next step, and confirm by checking 12*21 + 1 = 253.

workedExamples.question: Why is 1584 / 12 a good longer-number pattern?
workedExamples.method: The same flag logic extends left to right through more digits, and the answer 132 checks exactly because 12*132 = 1584.

workedExamples.question: How do you decimalise the remainder in 10 / 12 after the whole-number part?
workedExamples.method: 10 / 12 is 0 remainder 10. Continue with zeros, so 100 / 12 = 8 remainder 4, then 40 / 12 = 3 remainder 4, giving 0.83...

starterPractice: Warm-up: solve 132 / 11, 143 / 11, and 156 / 12 by stating the quotient first and then checking the dividend rebuild.
Remainder-control practice: solve 253 / 12, 275 / 12, and 169 / 13 by keeping the remainder smaller than the divisor.
Longer-number practice: solve 1584 / 12 and 1716 / 13 by saying the running quotient build before the final check.
Decimal practice: continue 10 / 12 and 7 / 12 into decimal form by carrying the remainder forward with zeros.

onboarding.coachIntro: Raj checks language comfort, current confidence, and session goal before starting The Crowning Gem (Advanced Division).
onboarding.placementRule: Recommended start level for Lesson 16: confident. If the learner struggles twice in one step, keep the pace slow and repeat the pattern with a smaller number.

mission.missionPromise: Use one-line division by two-figure divisors.
mission.successCelebration: Celebrate each correct step in The Crowning Gem (Advanced Division) with points, a badge pulse, and a quick coach line before moving on.

microLessonPattern: Coach opens with one short hook and names the pattern.
Coach models one worked move on the board.
Coach reads the exercise question aloud.
Niagh tries before the full answer is shown.
Instant feedback either celebrates or repairs the first mistake.
A quick review prompt decides whether the learner advances or repeats.

rewardLoop.xpUnit: Award 10 to 20 XP per exercise group based on the step position in the lesson path.
rewardLoop.streakRule: Keep the streak visible on every step and protect it with immediate retries instead of long explanations.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each exercise group has one badge focus tied to the subtopic being learned.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Short praise, points pulse, and progress-bar movement after every correct response.

reviewLoop.trigger: If the learner answers incorrectly, hesitates, or shows low confidence, reopen the same pattern with one smaller follow-up.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Use the micro-practice line as the first repair loop before advancing.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance only after the learner can answer the checkpoint and complete one try in the same subtopic.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Weak steps should return in the next session as review cards before new content.

uiDirectives.noScrollGoal: The learner should see mission progress, the current question, and the main action buttons without long vertical scrolling.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Single flag division with exact answers
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise A: Single flag division with exact answers
sessionFlow.coachHook: A one-flag divisor such as 11 or 12 can be handled in one running line: bring down the first quotient digit and let the flag control the next step.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 132 / 11, 143 / 11, and 156 / 12, keeping the flag digit visible beside the divisor.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How does a one-flag divisor such as 11 or 12 control the next quotient digit?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, say the first quotient digit and then the next running step.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How does a one-flag divisor such as 11 or 12 control the next quotient digit?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You used the one-flag pattern to get an exact answer.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Bring down the first quotient digit, then let the flag guide the next step.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: solve 132 / 11 and 143 / 11 by saying the running quotient build aloud.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise B: Single flag division with remainder
sessionFlow.coachHook: The same one-flag pattern works with remainders, but the remainder must stay smaller than the divisor and should be checked immediately.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 253 / 12 and 169 / 13, then rebuild each dividend from divisor times quotient plus remainder.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why must the remainder in one-flag division be checked against the divisor at the end?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, give the quotient, the remainder, and then the check.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why must the remainder in one-flag division be checked against the divisor at the end?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You kept the remainder valid and confirmed it by checking.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The remainder must stay smaller than the divisor and must rebuild the dividend correctly.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: solve 253 / 12 and 169 / 13, then check both answers.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise C: Short division remainder control
sessionFlow.coachHook: Remainder control matters in short advanced division: the running answer is not finished until the remainder is normalized and checked.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 275 / 12, 298 / 13, and 347 / 12 with quotient, remainder, and check side by side.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do you know the remainder is under control in short advanced division?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, say when the quotient is fixed and what must still be checked about the remainder.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do you know the remainder is under control in short advanced division?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You treated remainder control as part of the method, not an afterthought.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Do not stop until the remainder is smaller than the divisor and the check works.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: solve 275 / 12 and 298 / 13, then explain why the remainder is acceptable.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise D: Short division check and repair
sessionFlow.coachHook: A fast check catches most mistakes immediately: multiply divisor by quotient, add the remainder, and confirm the original dividend.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 347 / 12 and 425 / 13, showing the rebuild line under the quotient and remainder.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why is divisor times quotient plus remainder the fastest repair check for short advanced division?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, solve the division and then say the rebuild line.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why is divisor times quotient plus remainder the fastest repair check for short advanced division?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You used the check to confirm the advanced division instead of trusting the first pass blindly.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The rebuild check is the quickest proof that the answer is right.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: solve 347 / 12 and 425 / 13, then rebuild the dividend in one line.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Longer dividends still follow the same flag logic, but the running quotient has more positions, so the board layout must stay disciplined.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 1584 / 12 and 1716 / 13 with the running quotient written left to right and the final check below.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How does the one-flag pattern extend from short division to longer-number division?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, say the running quotient build before the final answer.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How does the one-flag pattern extend from short division to longer-number division?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You kept the same method while extending it through more digits.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: The logic is the same; only the running quotient line gets longer.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: solve 1584 / 12 and 1716 / 13 by saying the running quotient build aloud.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Longer number division with exact answers
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise F: Longer number division with exact answers
sessionFlow.coachHook: Exact longer divisions are the cleanest way to see the pattern because the check closes with zero remainder and exposes the quotient structure clearly.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 1848 / 12 and 2002 / 11, emphasizing the final exact check.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why are exact longer divisions useful when learning the advanced division pattern?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, solve the exact division and then say why the zero remainder matters.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why are exact longer divisions useful when learning the advanced division pattern?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. The exact answer made the running structure easier to verify.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: A zero remainder makes the pattern and the check easier to see.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: solve 1848 / 12 and 2002 / 11, then explain why exact cases are good training.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Negative flag digits with bar numbers
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise G: Negative flag digits with bar numbers
sessionFlow.coachHook: When the flagged correction is negative, bar-number thinking keeps the subtraction pattern visible and prevents sign mistakes.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 2211 / 112 and 1443 / 111, marking the negative flag and the subtractive correction clearly.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Why do negative flag digits change the running correction in advanced division?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, say why the correction is subtractive before you compute the next step.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Why do negative flag digits change the running correction in advanced division?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You treated the bar-number flag as a subtractive instruction.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: A negative flag means the running correction must be subtracted, not added.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: explain the subtractive flag in 2211 / 112 and check 1443 / 111.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Negative flag checks and mixed signs
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise H: Negative flag checks and mixed signs
sessionFlow.coachHook: Above-base divisors still end with the same check line, but sign control matters more because one mistaken addition can spoil the whole quotient.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Work 1345 / 112 and 1554 / 111, then rebuild the dividend from divisor times quotient plus remainder.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do you prevent sign mistakes when using negative flag digits?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, say the sign rule first and then solve the next step.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do you prevent sign mistakes when using negative flag digits?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You controlled the sign and then confirmed it with a rebuild check.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: State the sign rule aloud before computing the correction.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: solve 1345 / 112 and 1554 / 111, then verify by rebuilding the dividend.

sessionFlow.coachHook: When the whole-number quotient is finished, the remainder can keep going by bringing down zeros. The advanced division pattern continues into the decimal places.
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Show 10 / 12 and 7 / 12 continuing beyond the whole-number answer into decimal digits, with each zero brought down explicitly.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: How do you extend advanced division into decimals after the whole-number quotient is finished?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Niagh, say what happens to the remainder first and then give the next decimal digit.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: How do you extend advanced division into decimals after the whole-number quotient is finished?
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct. You carried the remainder forward into decimal form without changing the core pattern.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Bring down a zero and keep the same division logic going.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Micro-practice: continue 10 / 12 and 7 / 12 into decimals by carrying the remainder forward with zeros.
